question.problem: Which value of $n$ satisfies the equation $\frac{3}{2n}-\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}=\frac{7}{3n}?$
question.worked_solution:
We note that $n=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $2n,$ ${n}^{2},$ and $3n.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(2n,{n}^{2},3n)=6{n}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $6{n}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2n}-\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}} & =\frac{7}{3n} \\ 6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2n}-\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}) & =6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{7}{3n}) \\ 6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2n})-6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}) & =6{n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{7}{3n}) \\ 3n\cdot 2n\cdot (\frac{3}{2n})-6\cdot {n}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1-n}{{n}^{2}}) & =2n\cdot 3n\cdot (\frac{7}{3n}) \\ 3n\cdot \cancel{2n}\cdot (\frac{3}{\cancel{2n}})-6\cdot \cancel{{n}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1-n}{\cancel{{n}^{2}}}) & =2n\cdot \cancel{3n}\cdot (\frac{7}{\cancel{3n}}) \\ 3n\cdot (3)-6\cdot (1-n) & =2n\cdot (7) \\ 9n-6(1-n) & =14n\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $n,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}9n-6(1-n) & =14n \\ 15n-6 & =14n \\ n & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $n=0$ as a solution. But since $n=6\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $n=6.$
